there are obstacles for general practitioners to identify mental disorders at outpatient departments in developing countries, and the key to overcoming these challenges lies in support of changes to policy, programs and utilization of tools.
GPs’ ability to diagnose and treat mental disorders is limited by their lack of confidence, skills, and knowledge, and by their lack of access to tools, training, and support.
GPs in developing country settings have difficulties in making psychiatric diagnoses and systematic evaluation, which can be overcome by optimizing strategies.

GPs’ identification of mental disorders in outpatient settings.
GPs’ difficulties in identifying mental disorders and proposes optimized strategies.
the identification of mental disorders by GPs and proposes strategies for overcoming obstacles.

GPs need to be trained in the diagnosis and evaluation of mental disorders, and that the training should be based on the above strategies.
it is difficult to identify mental disorders in outpatient departments in developing countries without external help.

it is important to strengthen GPs’ ability to diagnose and evaluate mental disorders, to provide support for their diagnosis, and to improve the quality of psychiatric evaluation and reevaluation in order to improve their ability to diagnose and identify mental disorders.

GPs’ identification of mental disorders can be enhanced through the combination of these strategies.

the development of GPs in the diagnosis and treatment of mental disorders is a process of gradual improvement.
the government should provide support to improve the quality of psychiatric training for GPs and the quality of mental health services in primary care.
